checks.message: Secret not encrypted with a customer managed KMS key
checks.context: By default, Secrets Manager uses the AWS managed key (aws/secretsmanager). Using a customer managed KMS key gives you full control over key rotation, access policies, and an audit trail of every decryption via CloudTrail.

checks.message: Verify you are not storing plaintext credentials in --secret-string
checks.context: The --secret-string value is logged in CloudTrail and shell history. Use a JSON structure for structured secrets and avoid passing raw passwords directly on the command line.

checks.message: Secret deletion has a recovery window. Verify no applications depend on it
checks.context: By default, secrets are scheduled for deletion after 30 days (minimum is 7 days). Applications still referencing this secret will fail immediately. Use --force-delete-without-recovery only if you are certain the secret is unused.

checks.message: Recovery window not explicitly set. Defaults to 30 days, but should be confirmed
checks.context: Setting the maximum recovery window (30 days) gives you time to discover any applications that depend on the secret before it is permanently destroyed.

checks.message: Ensure all applications are updated to fetch the new secret value after rotation
checks.context: Secret rotation changes the secret value immediately. Applications that cache credentials will fail until they refresh. Ensure your rotation Lambda function handles the AWSPENDING, AWSCURRENT, and AWSPREVIOUS stages correctly.

checks.message: Enable automatic key rotation after creation with `aws kms enable-key-rotation`
checks.context: Key rotation is not a flag on create-key; it requires a separate API call. AWS recommends enabling automatic annual rotation for all customer managed KMS keys. Key rotation limits the blast radius if a key is ever compromised, and is required by many compliance frameworks.

checks.message: Review the key policy for wildcard principals
checks.context: A KMS key policy with Principal:* grants any AWS principal access to the key. This can allow unintended decryption of encrypted data. Always scope key policies to specific accounts, roles, or users.

checks.message: KMS key deletion is permanent. All data encrypted with this key will be unrecoverable
checks.context: Once a KMS key is deleted, any data encrypted with it (S3 objects, RDS databases, EBS volumes, Secrets Manager secrets) becomes permanently inaccessible. There is no way to recover the key or the data.

checks.message: No pending window specified. Defaults to 30 days, but should be set explicitly
checks.context: The waiting period is 7–30 days; the default is 30 days. Set this explicitly so the window is intentional. Use the maximum (30 days) to give yourself the most time to identify all services and data that depend on this key before it is irreversibly destroyed.

checks.message: Disabling a KMS key will immediately break all services using it
checks.context: Disabling a KMS key prevents all encrypt/decrypt operations. Any service using this key (S3, RDS, EBS, Secrets Manager) will fail immediately. Identify all key users before disabling.

checks.message: Verify the new key policy does not lock out all administrators
checks.context: A misconfigured KMS key policy can lock out all IAM users and roles, making the key permanently unmanageable. Always ensure the key policy includes at least one admin principal with kms:PutKeyPolicy permission.

checks.message: Shield Advanced is $3,000/month with a 1-year commitment — verify this is intentional
checks.context: Evaluate your actual DDoS risk profile before subscribing. For most workloads, Shield Standard (free) plus WAF is sufficient. Shield Advanced makes sense for high-profile public-facing services.

checks.message: Associate a Route 53 health check for health-based detection
checks.context: Without a health check, Shield Advanced can't distinguish a DDoS attack from a legitimate traffic spike. A health check enables proactive engagement with the AWS DDoS Response Team.

checks.message: Enable all data sources — S3 protection, EKS audit logs, and malware protection are off by default
checks.context: A detector with only CloudTrail and VPC flow logs misses S3 data events, Kubernetes API activity, EC2 malware scanning, Lambda network activity, and RDS login events. Most features are enabled by default when you create a detector, but explicitly specifying them ensures they are not accidentally omitted. Use --features to enumerate all protection plans you want enabled.

checks.message: Deleting a GuardDuty detector removes all threat detection for this region
checks.context: All findings, suppression rules, and threat intelligence are destroyed. Disabling GuardDuty is one of the first things attackers do after gaining access. Verify this is intentional.

checks.message: Disassociating removes this account's findings from the central security console
checks.context: Your security team's GuardDuty administrator account will no longer see findings from this account. Threats in this account become invisible to centralized monitoring.

checks.message: Validation method not specified. Defaults to EMAIL, which is fragile and doesn't auto-renew
checks.context: Email validation sends to WHOIS contacts that are often wrong or outdated. DNS validation is automated, doesn't expire, and auto-renews without manual intervention. Always explicitly set --validation-method DNS.

checks.message: Verify the certificate is not in use before deleting
checks.context: Deleting a certificate still associated with a CloudFront distribution, ALB, or API Gateway causes HTTPS to fail immediately. ACM warns you if it's in use, but verify manually.

checks.message: The private key must never be stored in git, S3 without encryption, or shared via chat
checks.context: Importing a certificate requires the private key on the command line. That key must be stored in Secrets Manager or KMS-encrypted storage — not in your shell history or a text file.

checks.message: Validation emails are sent to WHOIS contacts — verify the domain owner will receive them
checks.context: If the WHOIS contacts are outdated or incorrect, the validation email will go to the wrong person. Consider switching to DNS validation for automated, reliable certificate issuance.

checks.message: Malware scan creates a snapshot of the EBS volume — verify the instance is in a supported region
checks.context: GuardDuty malware protection creates an EBS snapshot for scanning. This incurs snapshot storage costs. Scans can take minutes to hours depending on volume size.
